content: During vaginal delivery, between 1% and 8% of women experience third-degree perineal tears, which involve injury to the anal sphincter, or fourth-degree perineal tears, which extend to the rectal mucosa. These types of tears are more frequently observed following forceps-assisted deliveries (28%) and midline episiotomies. Such injuries are at risk of bacterial contamination from the rectum, which significantly increases the likelihood of perineal wound infections. The use of prophylactic antibiotics has been proposed as a potential strategy to prevent these infections. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of prophylactic antibiotics in reducing maternal morbidity and associated complications in cases of thirdand fourth-degree perineal tears during vaginal birth. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of August 31, 2014), along with a review of reference lists from relevant articles. The study included randomized controlled trials that compared the outcomes of prophylactic antibiotic administration versus placebo or no antibiotics in women with thirdor fourth-degree perineal tears. Data collection and analysis were performed independently by two reviewers, who assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and ensured the accuracy of the extracted data. Only one trial met the inclusion criteria. This trial involved 147 women, although the pre-planned sample size was 310. It compared the effects of a single intravenous dose of a second-generation cephalosporin (either cefotetan or cefoxitin, 1 g) with a placebo on postpartum perineal wound complications. At the two-week postpartum follow-up, the incidence of perineal wound complications (including wound disruption and purulent discharge) was 8.20% in the antibiotic group compared to 24.10% in the placebo group. This corresponds to a risk ratio (RR) of 0.34, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.12 to 0.96, suggesting a significant reduction in complications with antibiotic use. However, the high rate of missed follow-up appointments limits the generalizability of these findings. The overall risk of bias in the trial was low, except for issues related to incomplete outcome data. Using the GRADE system, the quality of evidence was rated as moderate for infection rates at two weeks postpartum and low for infection rates at six weeks postpartum. In conclusion, while the data indicate that prophylactic antibiotics may reduce perineal wound complications following thirdor fourth-degree perineal tears, the high rate of loss to follow-up necessitates cautious interpretation of the results. These findings are based on a single, small-scale trial, and further research is needed to confirm the benefits of this intervention.
